Population surveys of the Slender emperor (Lethrinus variegatus) on the Great Barrier Reef indicate that individuals reach sexual maturity upon attaining a total length of approximately 10 cm [Lp = approximately 10 cm]. The corresponding body mass at this developmental milestone is estimated at 14 grams [Wwp = 14 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions for this species. This size at puberty is relatively modest compared to the maximum total length recorded for this species, which reaches 20 cm [Li = 20 cm]. Field studies show that reproductively active adults can achieve an ultimate wet weight of 111.5 grams [Wwi = 111.5 grams], representing a roughly eightfold increase in mass from the point of sexual maturation to maximum size. The length at first reproduction often coincides closely with the length at puberty, a pattern common among smaller-bodied lethrinids that inhabit shallow coral reef flats. These values were collected from specimens measured during routine fishery-independent monitoring programs across the central Indo-Pacific region.

The gonadosomatic index (GSI) of Lethrinus variegatus was quantified at 12% [GSI = 12%] at a water temperature of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C]. The thermal regime of the habitat, which averages approximately this temperature throughout much of the year, appears to facilitate sustained gonadal recrudescence and oocyte development.

Neonates of Lethrinus variegatus emerge as small, pelagic yolk-sac larvae following chorion rupture, with an estimated wet weight at birth of 0.00018 grams [Wwb = 0.00018 grams]. This extremely low initial mass is derived from the typical egg diameter of related species and falls within the range expected for small-bodied lethrinids producing planktonic eggs. The yolk-dependent larva relies entirely on endogenous reserves during the first several days post-hatching, a period during which it undergoes rapid morphological differentiation. The transition to exogenous feeding begins as the mouth gapes open and retinal differentiation permits prey detection, marking a critical life-history bottleneck where larval survival hinges on the availability of suitable microzooplankton. Mortality during these early stages is notoriously high, as the tiny larvae are vulnerable to a wide array of planktivorous predators.

The maximum longevity of Lethrinus variegatus has been estimated at approximately 5475 days [am = approximately 5475 days] for individuals living at a sustained temperature of 27.9 °C [T = 27.9 °C]. This lifespan represents the sum of fifteen reproductive cycles and is consistent with the moderate pace of life observed in other small-bodied emperors. Oldest documented individuals are typically recovered from protected reef flats where fishing pressure is minimal and habitat complexity provides ample refuge from piscivorous predators. The species' iteroparous reproductive strategy, involving repeated spawning events across multiple seasons, is well-suited to this lifespan, allowing individuals to buffer against poor recruitment years. Age validation studies using sectioned otoliths have confirmed annual increment formation under the stable thermal conditions typical of tropical waters, lending confidence to these longevity estimates.

Mark-recapture studies of Lethrinus variegatus have provided valuable insight into growth trajectories, indicating that the length at puberty of 10 cm [Lp = 10 cm] is typically attained within the first two years of life. Individuals continue to add somatic tissue steadily thereafter, eventually approaching the asymptotic total length of 20 cm [Li = 20 cm] by approximately age five or six. The corresponding ultimate wet weight of 111.5 grams [Wwi = 111.5 grams] is achieved only by the largest, oldest individuals, with most adults weighing between 60 and 90 grams. This growth pattern is characteristic of a species that allocates considerable energetic resources to reproduction early in life rather than delaying maturity to achieve a larger body size. The relatively small maximum size likely reflects the selective pressures of life on shallow coral reefs, where shelter availability and gape-limited predation shape body size evolution in the lethrinid lineage.
